notes: Parent kinds: explicit = the notes state the link; component = the parent introduced the child; sequence = chronological predecessor in the lineage. year null = the notes do not date the framework.

nodes.name: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision formed
introduced: G10 central bankers' committee for standardised global bank regulation
responding_to: Self-regulating bank consortiums failed during financial panics
1960s-70s trade growth needed coordinated financial regulation
Interconnected global banks posed risks to multiple economies
nodes.summary: G10 central bankers create the body that writes every later Basel accord.

nodes.name: Basel I

parent_links.basis: The BCBS introduced Basel I in 1988

introduced: Minimum capital requirements based on risk exposures
Tier 1 core and Tier 2 supplementary capital
On-balance-sheet risk weights of 0%, 20%, 50% and 100%
Credit conversion factors for off-balance-sheet items
Current exposure method: max(V, 0) plus a notional add-on
restricted: Tier 1 capital must exceed 4% of RWA
Total capital must exceed 8% of RWA
Goodwill subtracted from equity in Tier 1
Equity and commodity derivative risk weights capped at 50%
responding_to: Need to better gauge bank capital adequacy
nodes.summary: First global minimum: capital held against credit-risk-weighted assets.

nodes.name: Basel II

parent_links.basis: Basel II answers named Basel I limitations

introduced: Three pillars: minimum capital, supervisory review, market discipline
Standardised credit risk weights based on credit ratings
IRB capital: one-year 99.9% VaR, net of expected loss
First capital charges for operational risk
BIA, standardised and AMA routes to op-risk capital
ICAAP introduced under Pillar 2
Pillar 3 disclosure of capital, exposures and risk measures
Seven Level 1 operational-risk event types
Pillar 2 extra capital for concentration, compliance, governance risks
restricted: Kept the 8% total capital ratio
OECD status no longer sets risk weights
IRB probability of default floored at 0.03%
Foundation IRB LGD fixed: 45% senior, 75% subordinated
Foundation IRB maturity fixed at 2.5 years
responding_to: Basel I ignored creditworthiness: every loan weighted 100%
Basel I ignored diversification and default correlation
nodes.summary: Risk-sensitive capital: ratings, internal models, an op-risk charge and three pillars.

nodes.name: Basel III
nodes.year_note: Not dated in the notes; placed by its parents/lineage only.

parent_links.basis: Basel III raised the Basel II 8% minimum to 10.5%

introduced: Common Equity Tier 1 minimum of 4.5% of RWA
Additional Tier 1 of 1.5%, total Tier 1 6%
Conservation buffer: 7% CET1, 8.5% Tier 1, 10.5% total
Countercyclical buffer of 0% to 2.5% of RWA
G-SIB buffers of 1% to 3.5%
Categorisation and stricter rules for SIFIs
Counterparty credit risk management requirements
restricted: Tier 3 capital eliminated
Focus on tangible Tier 1 capital
Capital cut for pension deficits and group cross-holdings
Limits on exposures to single counterparties
Minimum capital ratio raised from 8% to 10.5%
responding_to: Banks needing protection in times of financial distress
Bank cyclicality feeding credit bubbles and instability
G-SIB failures' significant impact on the global system
nodes.summary: Post-crisis rebuild: more and better capital, plus conservation and systemic buffers.

nodes.name: Basel III leverage ratio
nodes.year_note: Not dated in the notes; placed by its parents/lineage only.

parent_links.basis: Basel III introduced leverage ratios

introduced: Ratio of capital to total exposure
Exposure includes off-balance-sheet items like loan commitments
restricted: Minimum leverage ratio of 3%
nodes.summary: A 3% floor on capital against all exposure, on and off the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Basel III finalisation (December 2017 reforms)

parent_links.basis: The December 2017 reforms revise the Basel III framework
The 2017 reforms revise the leverage ratio framework

introduced: Output floor: RWA at least 72.5% of standardised RWA
Input floors for PD, LGD and EAD
Leverage ratio buffer for G-SIBs, met with Tier 1
More granular SA risk weights, e.g. mortgages by LTV
CVA framework aligned with market risk via fair-value sensitivities
Leverage exposure better captures derivatives and off-balance-sheet items
restricted: Advanced IRB barred for large corporates and financial institutions
IRB approach for CVA removed
Internal models restricted for credit, CVA and op risk
Reduced reliance on external credit ratings
responding_to: Internal-model banks cut capital far below standardised levels
Internal models gave banks an unfair capital advantage
Basel II floor not robust or risk-sensitive enough

keywords: Removed the IRB approach for CVA
Restricting the use of internal model

nodes.summary: Constrains internal models: output floor, input floors, fewer model options.

nodes.name: 1996 Market Risk Amendment

parent_links.basis: An amendment to Basel I adding market risk
The 1995 amendment had not addressed market risk

introduced: Capital held against market risk from trading activities
Standardised approach with preset charges per trading-book item
Internal models: 10-day VaR at 99% confidence
Market RWA = 12.5 x max(VaR(t-1), m x average VaR)
Backtest one-day 99% VaR over the previous 250 days
Green, yellow and red backtesting zones
restricted: Multiplier at least 3, rising to 4 in the red zone
Ten or more exceptions put the bank in the red zone
Standardised approach ignores correlations between instruments
responding_to: 1987 crash and VaR's popularity exposed market-risk gaps
The 1995 amendment had not addressed market risk
nodes.summary: Brings trading-book market risk into capital, via VaR models or standard charges.

nodes.name: Basel 2.5 (Basel II.5)

parent_links.basis: Stressed VaR added on top of the Basel I VaR measure
The response to Basel II in the 2007-2009 crisis

introduced: Stressed VaR from a 250-day period of stressed markets
Stressed VaR added on top of current VaR
Incremental risk charge covering downgrades as well as defaults
Comprehensive risk measure for correlation-dependent credit products
IRC liquidity horizons with constant-level-of-risk assumption
restricted: Unrated or below-BB- positions carry a 100% capital charge
Capital adds a multiplied stressed-VaR term to the VaR term
responding_to: Crisis showed Basel II own estimates underestimated risk
Low trading-book capital drew risky assets out of the banking book
Crisis losses from downgrades, spreads, illiquidity, not just defaults
nodes.summary: Crisis patch on the 1996 VaR: stressed VaR, IRC for migration, CRM for correlation books.

nodes.name: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book

parent_links.basis: FRTB replaces the Basel II.5 stressed VaR with stressed ES

source_keywords: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
introduced: Stressed expected shortfall at 97.5% replaces VaR
Five liquidity horizons: 10, 20, 60, 120, 250 days
Nested ES shocks scaled by square root of horizon differences
Revised SA: sensitivities, default risk charge, residual risk add-on
Seven risk classes, three of them credit spread
Desk-level backtesting at both 99% and 97.5%
P&L attribution tests for bias and noise
Default risk charge: 99.9% one-year VaR, equities included
restricted: Positions cannot be reclassified between trading and banking books
Capital benefit from switching books is disallowed
Trading-book entry needs ability to trade and desk risk management
More than 12 (99%) or 30 (97.5%) exceptions force SA
PLA breaches on four or more occasions force SA
Securitisations must use the standardised approach
IRC constant-risk replacement assumption dropped
responding_to: VaR says nothing about losses beyond the threshold
Lower trading-book capital invited boundary regulatory arbitrage
Own-model CRM gave varying capital for the same portfolio
nodes.summary: Rebuilds market-risk capital: stressed ES, liquidity horizons, desk-level model approval.
aliases: Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk

nodes.name: 1995 Basel I amendment (netting)

parent_links.basis: Revised Basel I, which had discouraged hedging

introduced: Bilateral netting of credit exposures for regulatory capital

changes.text: G10 central bankers set up a standing committee to standardise global bank regulation.
changes.why: The committee was formed first (1974); its first accord came in 1988.

changes.text: Response to banks interconnected across economies after 1960s-70s trade growth.
changes.why: Cross-border banking risk prompted the committee itself, before any accord.

changes.text: First sets a 4% Tier 1 and 8% total capital minimum against risk-weighted assets.
changes.why: Basel I set 4%/8%; Basel II kept the 8%; Basel III raised the total to 10.5%.

changes.text: Uninsured residential mortgages get a 50% risk weight; corporate loans 100%.
changes.why: The fixed four-bucket weight table is Basel I's Figure 60.1.

changes.text: Claims on OECD governments, cash and gold carry a zero risk weight.
changes.why: OECD status drove Basel I weights; Basel II dropped it for ratings.

changes.text: Guarantees convert to on-balance-sheet equivalents at 100%, standby letters of credit at 50%.
changes.why: Credit conversion factors are part of the original Basel I rules.

changes.text: Derivative credit exposure = max(current value, 0) plus a notional-based add-on.
changes.why: The current exposure method came with Basel I; 1995 added netting to it.

changes.text: Bilateral netting of derivative credit exposures is recognised for regulatory capital.
changes.why: Basel I discouraged hedging; netting was allowed in 1995.

changes.text: Add-on becomes 0.4 x D plus 0.6 x D x (netted over gross current exposure).
changes.why: The NRR-weighted add-on is the 1995 netting formula.

changes.text: Add-on factors introduced for equity and commodity derivatives.
changes.why: Original Basel I did not cover them; the 1995 amendment added add-ons.

changes.text: Add-on table gains a maturity bucket for contracts longer than five years.
changes.why: The notes date the extra maturity bucket to the 1995 revision.

changes.text: Banks must measure market risk in trading activities and hold capital against it.
changes.why: Market risk capital arrived in 1996; the 1995 step was netting only.

changes.text: Internal models may set capital using 10-day VaR at 99% confidence.
changes.why: Plain 10-day 99% VaR is the 1996 model; 2.5 added stressed VaR, FRTB moved to ES.

changes.text: Market RWA equals 12.5 times the larger of yesterday's VaR and m times average VaR.
changes.why: This is the 1996 market capital formula; Basel 2.5 adds a stressed-VaR term.

changes.text: One-day 99% VaR backtested over 250 days; exceptions raise the capital multiplier.
changes.why: Bank-wide backtesting with a multiplier is 1996; FRTB backtests desk by desk.

changes.text: Ten or more backtesting exceptions in a year put the multiplier at 4.
changes.why: The green/yellow/red zones set the multiplier from 3 to 4.

changes.text: Zero to four exceptions: green zone, multiplier stays at 3.
changes.why: Green-zone treatment is part of the VaR backtesting rules.

changes.text: Market risk capital based on VaR with a 10-day horizon and 99% confidence, recent losses only.
changes.why: MR-18 labels this first step "Basel I": VaR on current data.

changes.text: Credit risk weights now depend on external ratings, not OECD membership.
changes.why: The Basel II standardised approach made weights rating-based.

changes.text: Regulators fix LGD at 45% senior and 75% subordinated, and maturity at 2.5 years.
changes.why: Supervisory LGD and fixed maturity define the foundation IRB approach.

changes.text: First explicit capital charge for operational risk, e.g. 15% of average gross income.
changes.why: The Basic Indicator Approach (15%) is Basel II; SMA replaced it later.

changes.text: Supervisory review pillar introduces an internal capital adequacy assessment process.
changes.why: ICAAP arrives with Pillar 2 of Basel II.

changes.text: Banks must disclose capital structure, risk exposures and capital allocation to the market.
changes.why: Market discipline via disclosure is Pillar 3 of Basel II.

changes.text: Operational loss events classified into seven Level 1 event types.
changes.why: The seven event types are the Basel II categories; SMA reuses them.

changes.text: Supervisors may add capital for concentration, compliance and governance risks outside Pillar 1.
changes.why: Pillar 2 of Basel II reaches risks that Pillar 1 does not.

changes.text: IRB capital built on the Vasicek worst-case default rate at a high percentile.
changes.why: CR-10 ties Vasicek's WCDR to the Basel II IRB approach.

changes.text: Banks may build tailored internal models of operational risk from their own data.
changes.why: AMA, part of Basel II (2006), allowed internal op-risk models.

changes.text: Insurers hold a minimum capital requirement plus buffers forming a solvency capital requirement.
changes.why: MCR and SCR are the insurance regime, not a bank accord.

changes.text: Internal-model capital uses one-year VaR at 99.5% confidence.
changes.why: 99.5% one-year is the insurance internal model; Basel IRB uses 99.9%.

changes.text: VaR must also be computed on a 250-day period of stressed market conditions.
changes.why: Stressed VaR is Basel 2.5; FRTB later uses stressed ES instead.

changes.text: Trading-book default charge widened to capture downgrades and spread risk, not only defaults.
changes.why: The IRC expanded the IDRC after crisis losses came from downgrades.

changes.text: A single charge for correlation-dependent credit products such as ABS and CDOs.
changes.why: The comprehensive risk measure was introduced in Basel 2.5.

changes.text: Unrated or below BB- correlation positions need dollar-for-dollar capital.
changes.why: The 100% charge sits inside the Basel 2.5 CRM.

changes.text: Banks may use their own approved models for the securitisation correlation charge.
changes.why: Own-model CRM was Basel II.5; FRTB withdrew it.

changes.text: A stressed measure is added alongside, not instead of, the current VaR.
changes.why: Basel II.5 keeps current VaR and adds stressed VaR on top.

changes.text: Capital measure switches to expected shortfall at 97.5% over a stressed period.
changes.why: Both the measure (ES) and the confidence (97.5%) change here.

changes.text: Five liquidity horizons from 10 to 250 days assigned by asset category.
changes.why: Category liquidity horizons belong to the FRTB ES calculation.

changes.text: Once booked, positions cannot move between trading and banking book without keeping original capital.
changes.why: The fixed boundary and disallowed benefit target regulatory arbitrage.

changes.text: A desk with more than 12 exceptions at 99% loses internal-model approval.
changes.why: Desk-level backtesting with SA fallback is FRTB, not the 1996 bank-wide zones.

changes.text: Bias ratio of unexplained to actual P&L must stay within plus or minus 10%.
changes.why: P&L attribution is an FRTB model-eligibility test.

changes.text: Securitisations must use the standardised approach; internal models withdrawn.
changes.why: The motivation was inconsistent capital across banks, not leniency.

changes.text: Jump-to-default charge at 99.9% one-year VaR now applies to equities too.
changes.why: The IDR charge covering all risk assets is FRTB's credit change.

changes.text: Drops the assumption that deteriorated credit positions are replaced to keep risk constant.
changes.why: The constant-level-of-risk assumption was Basel 2.5 IRC; FRTB drops it.

changes.text: Common equity Tier 1 must be at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets.
changes.why: The CET1 layer and its 4.5% minimum come with Basel III.

changes.text: Tier 3 capital eliminated; focus shifts to tangible Tier 1.
changes.why: Capital-quality changes were the first Basel III step.

changes.text: Buffer of 0% to 2.5% of RWA set according to the economic cycle.
changes.why: The countercyclical buffer is Basel III.

changes.text: Normal-times minimums become 7% core equity, 8.5% Tier 1 and 10.5% total capital.
changes.why: These include the capital conservation buffer.

changes.text: Global systemically important banks hold extra capital buffers of 1% to 3.5%.
changes.why: G-SIB risk-based buffers are Basel III; 2017 added a G-SIB leverage buffer.

changes.text: Capital adjusted downward for pension plan deficits and group cross-holdings.
changes.why: Stricter capital definitions are part of Basel III.

changes.text: Minimum capital ratio raised from 8% to 10.5%.
changes.why: CR-5: 8% under Basel II, 10.5% under Basel III.

changes.text: Capital over total exposure, including off-balance-sheet loan commitments, must be at least 3%.
changes.why: A 3% capital-to-exposure floor, not a liquidity ratio.

changes.text: Total RWA must be at least 72.5% of RWA computed under standardised approaches.
changes.why: The revised output floor came with the December 2017 reforms.

changes.text: Advanced IRB withdrawn for large corporates and financial institutions; foundation IRB required.
changes.why: Restricting internal models was the 2017 theme.

changes.text: Floors imposed on bank-estimated PD, LGD and EAD inputs.
changes.why: Basel II floored only PD (0.03%); 2017 floors all three inputs.

changes.text: IRB approach for CVA risk removed; only standardised or basic approaches remain.
changes.why: Removing CVA internal models is part of the 2017 package.

changes.text: Global systemically important banks get an extra Tier 1 buffer on the capital-to-exposure ratio.
changes.why: The G-SIB leverage buffer was added in 2017, after the 3% ratio.

changes.text: Residential mortgage risk weights vary with loan-to-value under the standardised approach.
changes.why: Granular SA weights were a 2017 revision.

changes.text: Securitisation in the floor: SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA or a 1,250% risk weight.
changes.why: These are the output-floor approaches for securitisation.

changes.text: Op-risk capital built from a business indicator times bucket coefficients of 12%, 15%, 18%.
changes.why: Marginal BI coefficients define the business indicator component.

changes.text: Loss component equals 15 times average annual operational loss over ten years.
changes.why: The loss component feeds the internal loss multiplier.

changes.text: Banks in the smallest size bucket hold capital equal to the BI component alone.
changes.why: Bucket 1 banks skip the internal loss multiplier.

changes.text: Without five years of loss data, no internal loss multiplier is possible.
changes.why: The five-year data minimum is a condition of the new approach.

changes.text: Mandatory modelling for regulatory op-risk capital ends; modelling shifts to Pillar 2 ICAAP.
changes.why: Replacing AMA removed modelling from Pillar 1 op-risk capital.

changes.text: All banks use one standardised op-risk approach based on income and historical losses.
changes.why: The single op-risk approach is part of the December 2017 revisions.

changes.text: High-quality liquid assets must cover net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period.
changes.why: 30 days and HQLA mark the short-horizon ratio.

changes.text: Stress scenario: three-notch downgrade, partial deposit loss, complete loss of wholesale funding.
changes.why: This acute 30-day scenario defines the short-horizon ratio.

changes.text: Phased in from 60% in 2015 to 100% in 2019.
changes.why: The other ratio had a single 1 January 2018 start date.

changes.text: Tactical current-position metric: available liquidity against 30-day net cash outflows.
changes.why: LTR-9 lists this ratio among current liquidity position metrics.

changes.text: Available stable funding must cover required stable funding over a one-year period.
changes.why: One-year structural funding, not a 30-day buffer.

changes.text: Liabilities weighted by stability in the numerator; assets by how hard they are to liquidate.
changes.why: ASF on funding (numerator), RSF on assets (denominator).

changes.text: Implemented on 1 January 2018.
changes.why: The other liquidity ratio phased in over 2015-2019.

changes.text: Seventeen principle areas: governance, risk tolerance, measurement, funding diversification, stress testing.
changes.why: The BIS/BCBS principles cover 17 areas.

changes.text: Early-warning indicators may be qualitative or quantitative, e.g. rapid asset growth.
changes.why: The general firm-level EWI list with that wording is BCBS-2008.

changes.text: Use forward-looking metrics on balance-sheet structure and projected cash flows.
changes.why: This is Principle 5 of the BCBS Sound Principles.

changes.text: A bank owns its liquidity risk: robust framework, contingency funding plan and HQLA cushion.
changes.why: The first principle: the bank owns, the supervisor assesses.

changes.text: Early-warning indicators paired with event triggers tailored to the firm's liquidity profile.
changes.why: Event triggers are the Federal Reserve document's discriminator.

changes.text: The firm moves through progressive states of readiness as a liquidity event evolves.
changes.why: Progressive readiness is the Federal Reserve statement's language.

changes.text: Monitoring indicator: the daily maximum liquidity requirement.
changes.why: Intraday-only indicators belong to the 2012 BCBS document.

changes.text: Track intraday throughput and the timing of intraday payments.
changes.why: Throughput and payment timing are intraday indicators.

changes.text: Monitor intraday credit lines extended to financial-institution customers.
changes.why: Another intraday-only indicator.

changes.text: Warning signs when embedded triggers in callable debt or OTC derivatives near breach.
changes.why: Embedded product triggers are the OCC discriminator.

changes.text: A CAMELS component or composite rating downgrade counts as an early-warning indicator.
changes.why: CAMELS is a US bank rating; this EWI is in the OCC list.

changes.text: Reluctance of trust managers, money managers and public entities to place funds.
changes.why: This credit-sensitive fund-provider EWI is on the OCC list.

changes.text: Standardised OTC derivatives must be centrally cleared and traded on exchanges or electronic platforms.
changes.why: The 2009 leaders' commitment after Bear Stearns.

changes.text: OTC derivative trades must be reported to trade repositories.
changes.why: Trade reporting was one of the 2009 commitments.

changes.text: Initial and variation margin extended to OTC derivatives that cannot be centrally cleared.
changes.why: Bilateral collateral rules followed the clearing mandate in 2011.

changes.text: Aims to cut regulatory arbitrage between clearable and non-clearable OTC trades.
changes.why: Margin on non-cleared trades removes the incentive to avoid clearing.

changes.text: Bilateral trades, historically lightly margined, get margin rules similar to central clearing.
changes.why: Margin for bilateral trades is the non-cleared regime.

changes.text: Bespoke credit-based bilateral margining starts giving way to regulatory rules.
changes.why: CR-18: bilateral margining with regulatory rules being introduced.

changes.text: A council is created to identify and address risks to the entire financial system.
changes.why: FSOC was created by the US post-crisis statute.

changes.text: Banks that accept insured deposits face limits on proprietary trading.
changes.why: The Volcker Rule is part of the US statute.

changes.text: A consumer financial protection bureau ensures clear and fair consumer lending.
changes.why: CFPB was established by the US statute.

changes.text: Hedge fund advisers with at least $150 million must register with the SEC and appoint a CCO.
changes.why: The US post-GFC statute regulates the adviser.

changes.text: The 15-client private adviser exemption is eliminated.
changes.why: Title IV removed the exemption that the 1940 regime created.

changes.text: Funds with more than $1.5 billion AUM file systemic-risk reports quarterly.
changes.why: Form PF filing thresholds came with the US statute.

changes.text: Mortgage originators must verify ability to repay; qualified mortgages are presumed compliant.
changes.why: CFPB rules from the US statute address retail credit risk.

changes.text: US statute protecting whistleblowers and regulating OTC derivatives.
changes.why: Whistleblower protection is in the US statute, not MiFID.

changes.text: Advisers with fewer than 15 clients are exempt from SEC registration.
changes.why: The exemption dates from the 1940 regime; Dodd-Frank removed it.

changes.text: EU rules require manager registration, detailed reporting and leverage limits for alternative funds.
changes.why: The EU regulates the manager and the leverage.

changes.text: Marketing rules for non-EU funds targeting EU investors; member states enforce.
changes.why: ESMA interprets the directive; member states enforce it.

changes.text: EU rules on proper business conduct, disclosure and reporting to prevent market abuse.
changes.why: The 2007 original set the conduct baseline.

changes.text: Post-crisis EU rules on trader pay, conflicts of interest and best execution.
changes.why: The 2014 revision added pay, conflicts and best-execution rules.

changes.text: Intraday bond price and volume data, with a one-month delay for less liquid bonds.
changes.why: IM-16 attributes this data regime to the 2014 EU rules.

changes.text: Mandatory reporting of transaction costs.
changes.why: Transaction-cost reporting is part of the 2014 EU rules.

changes.text: ML/FT risk assessed at country, sector, bank and customer-relationship levels.
changes.why: Four-level ML/FT assessment is Basel Committee AML guidance.

changes.text: Enhanced due diligence for politically exposed persons and frequent cross-border transfers.
changes.why: Risk-based customer acceptance is AML guidance.

changes.text: A bank not using IT monitoring must document why and show alternatives work.
changes.why: Transaction monitoring expectations sit in the ML/FT guidance.

changes.text: Uniform group-wide policies applied globally, adjusting for stricter local laws.
changes.why: Cross-border group management of ML/FT risk.

changes.text: Contracts with foreign providers must be governed by the institution's own jurisdiction's law.
changes.why: One of the seventeen contract provisions.

changes.text: The primary service provider is accountable for all subcontracted work.
changes.why: Subcontracting provision of the guidance.

changes.text: Due diligence on providers' financial statements, internal controls and disaster recovery plans.
changes.why: Provider due diligence is objective (b) of the guidance.

changes.text: Validation must be performed by a team independent of the model developers.
changes.why: Independent validation is a core supervisory expectation.

changes.text: Vendor models need more sensitivity analysis and benchmarking; vendors must supply details.
changes.why: Third-party model validation guidance.

changes.text: Revalidation is required after major model changes.
changes.why: Outcomes analysis may force amendment and revalidation.

changes.text: Ongoing monitoring through process verification and benchmarking against other models.
changes.why: Ongoing monitoring is one of the validation elements.

changes.text: Independent model risk review would have exposed limits of the copula CDO-pricing model.
changes.why: ORR-16's lesson: model risk management would have caught this.

changes.text: Seven principles spanning governance, risk management, incident management and ICT.
changes.why: The BCBS issued seven resilience principles.

changes.text: EU act targeting ICT third-party risk, including cloud, with mandated penetration tests.
changes.why: CI-8 lists this among EU micro-oriented tools.

changes.text: Promotes digital finance while imposing IT requirements on financial institutions.
changes.why: ORR-1 describes the EU act this way (then proposed).

changes.text: Stress testing moves from single shocks to multi-factor macro scenarios across the whole firm.
changes.why: This is what the 2009 US program changed.

changes.text: Projected losses published for each bank across eight asset classes.
changes.why: Bank-level disclosure across eight asset classes was the 2009 program.

changes.text: Explicit post-stress common equity threshold to confirm the bank stays viable.
changes.why: Capital-adequacy focus arrived with the 2009 program.

changes.text: Bank holding companies above $50 billion must submit capital plans for Fed evaluation.
changes.why: The Capital Plan Rule, evaluated through the annual review.

changes.text: Only macro-scenario results published, not bank-level results.
changes.why: The 2011 review cut transparency versus 2009; 2012 restored it.

changes.text: Seven principles for an effective capital adequacy process, ending with board oversight.
changes.why: The seven CAP principles apply under the Capital Plan Rule.

changes.text: Downloadable data and a comparison of bank versus third-party loss estimates.
changes.why: The 2011 European tests, notably the Irish test.

changes.text: Higher-risk crypto exposures get a 1,250% risk weight on both long and short positions.
changes.why: Group 2 treatment in the proposed bank-exposure standard.

changes.text: Lower-risk crypto assets weighted similarly to, or below, traditional assets.
changes.why: Group 1 treatment in the proposed standard.

changes.text: Regulators prioritise resources toward jurisdictions with significant crypto presence.
changes.why: A consideration for regulators, not a bank capital rule.

changes.text: Regulators monitor developments, define the regulatory perimeter and coordinate domestically.
changes.why: The agenda organises regulators themselves.

changes.text: Regulators urged to close data gaps, update frameworks and strengthen supervision of AI.
changes.why: The 2024 report's closing agenda.

changes.text: Third-party dependency and service-provider concentration flagged as AI stability vulnerabilities.
changes.why: One of the five vulnerabilities the 2024 report assesses.

differences: Basel 2.5 uses 99% VaR; FRTB uses expected shortfall at 97.5%.
Basel 2.5 adds stressed VaR to current VaR; FRTB uses stressed ES.
Basel 2.5 CRM used approved own models; FRTB mandates SA for securitisations.
IRC assumed constant risk via replacement; FRTB drops replacement.
FRTB adds liquidity horizons of 10 to 250 days by category.
LCR covers a 30-day stress; NSFR a one-year horizon.
LCR numerator is HQLA; NSFR numerator is available stable funding.
LCR denominator is net cash outflows; NSFR's is required stable funding.
LCR phased in 2015-2019; NSFR implemented 1 January 2018.
Basel II offered BIA, standardised and AMA; SMA is one approach.
AMA allowed internal models; SMA is non-model-based.
AMA was flexible but hard to compare; SMA targets comparability and simplicity.
BIA used 15% of gross income; SMA scales BI by 12%-18%.
SMA adds a loss component: 15 times average annual losses.
Basel I weighted all corporate loans 100%; Basel II weights by creditworthiness.
Basel I keyed weights to OECD status; Basel II uses credit ratings.
Basel II adds an operational risk capital charge.
Basel II adds supervisory review (ICAAP) and market-discipline disclosure pillars.
Both keep the 8% total capital ratio.
Minimum total capital: 8% under Basel II, 10.5% under Basel III.
Basel III eliminates Tier 3 and focuses on tangible Tier 1.
Basel III adds conservation, countercyclical and G-SIB buffers.
Basel III adds a leverage ratio and liquidity requirements.
Basel III raised capital quality and buffers; 2017 constrained internal models.
2017 adds a 72.5% output floor on internal-model RWA.
2017 adds a G-SIB leverage ratio buffer to the 3% ratio.
2017 removes the IRB approach for CVA risk.
Basel II allowed advanced IRB; 2017 bars it for large corporates and FIs.
Basel II floored PD at 0.03%; 2017 floors PD, LGD and EAD.
2017 output floor is more robust than the Basel II floor.
Basel II weights by external ratings; 2017 reduces reliance on ratings.
1996 capital is VaR-based; Basel 2.5 adds stressed VaR from 250 stressed days.
Basel 2.5 adds an IRC for downgrades and defaults.
Basel 2.5 adds a CRM for correlation-sensitive products.
Both use a multiplier of 3 on average VaR in the examples.
SCAP 2009 disclosed bank-level losses; 2011 CCAR only macro results.
2012 CCAR returned to SCAP-level bank disclosure.
CCAR evaluates BHC capital plans under the Capital Plan Rule.
MiFID I dates from 2007; MiFID II from 2014.
MiFID II adds pay, conflicts, independent advice and best execution.
MiFID II was the post-2007-2009 crisis enhancement.
2008 gives the general firm-level EWI list; 2012 is intraday-only.
Daily maximum liquidity requirement belongs to 2012, not 2008.
Rapid asset growth is a 2008 EWI, not an intraday indicator.
SR 10-6 introduces event triggers and progressive states of readiness.
OCC 2012 targets embedded triggers in products like callable debt.
SR 10-6 is the Federal Reserve's; OCC 2012 is the Comptroller's Handbook.
2009 mandates central clearing for standardised OTC derivatives.
2011 sets collateral rules for derivatives that cannot be cleared.
Cleared trades absorb losses mainly via initial margin; bilateral mainly via capital.
1940 Act exempted advisers under 15 clients; Dodd-Frank removed that exemption.
Dodd-Frank requires SEC registration at $150m and a CCO.
Dodd-Frank adds Form PF reporting and FSOC monitoring.
The US regulates the adviser; the EU regulates manager and leverage.
AIFMD imposes leverage limits; ESMA interprets, member states enforce.
BCBS issued seven principles; DORA is an EU act, proposed in ORR-1.
DORA centres on ICT third-party and cloud risk, with penetration tests.
